title: Process Questions: Probing Thinking Through Elaboration [FREE RESOURCE]
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark presents process questions, follow-ups that ask students how or why they reached an answer, as a practical complement to explicit instruction. Drawing on Rosenshine's observations of effective teachers, he frames the answer as the starting point of questioning. He distinguishes process questions from surface checks, unanchored discussion prompts, guess-what-I-am-thinking probing and premature analysis, and lists what good ones look like. The research case rests on elaboration, citing Wexler and Karpicke, with the claim that explaining why something works can rival retrieval practice for retention. He sets four conditions for success (explicit, consistent, calmly enforced, rehearsed) and offers sentence stems as a classroom resource.
points: A process question is a warm follow-up that asks how or why a student got an answer, not whether it was correct.
Process questions go after instruction and modelling, anchored to just-taught content so they do not overload working memory.
Elaboration turns recalled knowledge into understanding that transfers and exposes misconceptions before they harden.
Four conditions make the habit work: explicit expectations, consistent use, calm follow-through and rehearsed fluency with sentence stems.
The piece lists what process questions are not, including surface follow-ups, vague open prompts and replacing explanation with questioning.
quotes: Process questioning means asking students to explain how or why they arrived at an answer — not just what the answer is.

Process questions sit quietly inside strong explicit teaching. And when used well, they help students make sense of what they know, articulate their thinking, and cement understanding in long-term memory.
Research shows that while explicit instruction and retrieval practice are essential, they are not sufficient on their own to produce deep understanding.

When teachers only ask factual questions, students can appear fluent while their deep understanding remains fragile. They may recall definitions, steps, or quotations, but struggle to explain relationships, justify decisions, or transfer learning to new contexts.

Studies examining elaboration show that asking students to explain why something works, or how an answer was reached, improves understanding and long-term retention — sometimes matching or even outperforming retrieval practice alone.

Process questions come after instruction and modelling, once students have something to think with. They focus attention on a narrow slice of reasoning — a specific step, decision, or justification — rather than demanding broad or abstract analysis. And because they are tightly anchored to just-taught content, they optimise cognitive load without overwhelming working memory.
Process questions are about making thinking visible, strengthening understanding, and helping students learn how to think — not just what to say.
